label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
**She always brought something**

First post here, so forgive me if I'm doing this wrong.

There's a thread every month where we share the moments from work that stay with you. I've read them for a long time and never posted anything myself. This month I feel like I have to.

Her name was Mrs. H. She was 84, from Poland, and she had been coming to our store since 2019. Every Thursday, a weekly blister pack, 11 medications. She would come in, we would go through the pack together, she would ask me about her blood pressure pills she had already asked me about the week before, and then she would leave.

I'm not going to put her last name or anything else that could identify her here. She passed away and privacy still matters, especially to her family.

She died on October 30. On November 9 her daughter Basia came in to return the unused blister packs and her glucometer. That's all she brought in. She stood at the counter for a while after.

Here is the part I can't get out of my head. Mrs. H. lived alone. Her husband died in 2021. She walked with a cane with tennis balls on the bottom, the kind that go squeaking on the floor and stop you dead in an aisle. Every single Thursday she brought me something. Poppy seed cake. Once a jar of home-made pickles I had absolutely no idea what to do with. And when Ramadan came around, she remembered. She told me not to eat her cake until sunset, and she wrapped it in foil with my name on it.

In 2023 her new doctor added a medication that interacted with her warfarin. I called the doctor, we sorted it out, and that was that, it was literally my job. But she went around telling everyone that I had saved her life. I kept telling her, that's just the job, anyone would have done the same. She never listened to me about that.

When Basia came in with the returns, she handed me a card. Inside, in her mother's handwriting, was something Mrs. H. had written a long time ago and never given me: *for my Arabic daughter*. She had been saving it.

I cried in the back room. Priya, my tech, covered the counter for about ten minutes without saying one word to me. Thank you, Priya.

I studied pharmacy in Egypt. My father was a pharmacist too, in a small town, and he knew every family on his street. When I moved to Canada I thought it would be different here, more business, less personal. It's not different. I don't know why I thought it would be.

We are not supposed to get attached. They tell you that in school, and they teach you pharmacology, and interactions, and how to counsel, and how to document, and nobody teaches you how to say goodbye to a patient. You see somebody every week for seven years and then one Thursday they are not there, and the Thursday after that you wait for the door to open and it doesn't.

I keep thinking about her daughter standing there with a glucometer in a bag, and about the fact that Mrs. H. had something for me every single week for years and I never once said thank you properly. I did say it. I just mean I never said it the way I would say it now.

So I wanted to ask: if you have a patient like her, someone who quietly became part of your week, your routine, your store — I'd really like to read about them. I think there are more of us than we admit.
